About

I am a mathematical physicist at the Harvard Center of Mathematical Sciences and Applications. I work at the interface of pure mathematics and theoretical physics, using tools such as homological algebra, algebraic geometry and category theory to understand the structure of quantum field theory. Some questions I keep returning to:

  • Dualities. Quantum field theories have unexpected dualities: electric–magnetic duality, particle–vortex duality, mirror symmetry. What rigorous mathematics follows from them?
  • Observables. The objects one can measure in a field theory often carry rich algebraic structure. When can the algebra of observables be understood completely, for instance through Lie algebra cohomology?
  • BPS objects. Solitons, instantons and other BPS objects organize themselves into rich algebraic structures, which tie partial differential equations to higher algebra and category theory.
  • Foundations. Rigorous frameworks for quantum field theory, from factorization algebras to functorial and axiomatic approaches.

I received my PhD from Rutgers in 2021 under Greg Moore, and was then a member of the Institute for Advanced Study, mentored by Edward Witten.

Visualizations I like

A recurring theme in geometry and physics is that algebra can be extracted from differential equations. One counts solutions of an equation (gradient flow lines, holomorphic curves, solitons and instantons in field theory) and organizes the counts into algebraic objects such as chain complexes, A∞ categories and L∞ algebras. The axioms they satisfy, such as ∂² = 0, follow from the geometry of the solutions: a family of solutions depending on one parameter has two ends, where the solution breaks into simpler pieces, and the contributions of the two ends cancel.
